title: The Car Wash in Winter
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 25 of 40
content:
The car wash sign flickered twice before the pump stopped.

Greg looked up from the change drawer.

"Oh, come on."

Outside, winter rain hammered the asphalt and turned the edges of the parking lot silver. We had exactly one customer waiting, and they were already reconsidering their decision to get a car washed in weather that seemed determined to wash it again for free.

I stepped out beneath the awning.

"The pump is down," I told them. "We can refund your token or hold it until we're working again."

They asked for the refund.

Reasonable.

Greg handed it over, then stared toward the machinery room with the tired expression of a man who had just been informed that his entire day would involve a wrench.

"We can probably fix it," he said.

"We?"

He looked at me.

"I mean, I can probably fix it."

"Do you know what's wrong?"

"Not yet."

"Then maybe we can start with that."

He sighed.

The car wash was an ordinary little business in Beach City, not a musical stage where charm could fill a missing part. Its winter income paid bills, and the pump had been making an uneven knocking sound for a week. Greg had promised three different people he would take care of it before the next cold spell.

He hadn't booked a mechanic.

I followed him to the equipment room. He opened the access door, saw a wet patch beneath the pipe, and immediately reached toward the motor.

"Greg."

He stopped.

"Power first."

"Right."

We shut the equipment down at the breaker and checked that the indicator had gone dark. I wasn't going to pretend either of us had training to repair a live motor in wet conditions. Greg found the maintenance number on a sticker inside the panel.

He stared at it.

"Do you want me to call?" I asked.

"I've been telling everybody I can handle this."

"You can handle calling a person who knows how to fix it."

He laughed, but it sounded tired.

"That's very clever."

"It's also practical."

We called. A technician named Alva could arrive after lunch, weather permitting. She told us not to run the machine again and asked us to photograph the leaking connection from a safe distance. We did.

The sign went to CLOSED FOR REPAIR.

Greg watched me write it.

"Think anybody's going to be mad?"

"Somebody might. They can still have a refund."

He looked toward the empty wash bay.

"It's just hard, you know? Everybody thinks I'm the guy who can improvise his way out of anything."

"That sounds more like what you think they think."

He looked at me.

"You're getting annoying."

"Learned from the best."

He smiled.

We had time before Alva arrived. I suggested lunch. Greg offered to make sandwiches, then spent ten minutes apologizing for not having the right bread. We ate what he had.

The rain moved in sheets across the windows.

"Can I ask something?" I said.

"Sure."

"When you told me you needed help, it sounded like you were afraid I'd be disappointed."

Greg stared at his sandwich.

"I like being the fun guy."

"You are the fun guy."

"Yeah, until something breaks. Then I feel like I have to be the guy who fixes it before anybody sees me worry."

I rested my elbow on the table.

"I see you worry."

"Yeah?"

"Yes. I like you anyway."

He laughed softly.

"That's embarrassing."

"Terribly."

I reached for his hand. He let me take it.

We had been careful about our relationship from the beginning: I had told him I was ethically non-monogamous and preferred polyamory, and he had said he wanted to keep choosing us without pretending I could never love anyone else. Practical care was part of that, too. I didn't want him using every repair as proof he deserved my time.

Alva arrived at two. She checked the disconnected system and found a failing pump seal. The motor itself had survived. The replacement part was available, but the bill would be higher than Greg had hoped.

He looked at the estimate.

"Could we just patch it?"

"Not safely for long," Alva said. "You'd spend more replacing wet components later."

Greg asked what the work included. She explained the seal, a pressure test, and a note about the old pipe that might need replacing after winter. He asked when the job could be finished without making her promise a miracle.

We approved the repair.

I held the umbrella while he paid the deposit.

He grinned at me.

"Very heroic."

"The umbrella?"

"The not-panicking part."

"That's a work in progress."

When Alva finished, the pump ran steadily. Greg watched the gauge instead of celebrating immediately. He asked her to show him where the next inspection point was, then wrote the date on the calendar.

The car wash opened for the final hour of daylight.

Two customers came. We refunded one old token and sold one new wash. The income did not pay for the repair. Greg recorded the difference instead of pretending the numbers would become friendly if he made enough jokes.

We closed on time.

Back at the van, he was quiet.

"Disappointed?" I asked.

"In the pump? Absolutely."

"In me?"

He looked startled.

"Never."

I smiled.

"Then perhaps you can extend me the same courtesy when I can't fix something."

He leaned toward me.

"That, I think I can do."

I kissed him, slow and warm, smelling rain on his jacket. He laughed against my mouth when the van's windshield wipers switched on by accident.

"Romantic soundtrack," he said.

"Very expensive."

We changed out of our wet clothes later and kept the rest of the evening private. Before bed Greg put the technician's card in the drawer beside his guitar picks.

The next morning the pump held pressure.

The sign stayed on.

No fireworks, no magical rescue, just a repaired machine and a person who had learned that asking for help did not make his love smaller.
